claims.claim: The economy is the social institution through which a society's resources — its goods and services — are managed; in practice this means producing, distributing, and consuming them.
A market economy (capitalism in OpenStax's terms) is an economic system based on private ownership, in which prices and wages are shaped by supply, demand, and competition.

A command economy (socialism in its state-run form, in OpenStax's terms) is an economic system in which the government owns goods and production and directs what is made, with the aim of sharing work and wealth more equally.
Real economies are mixed: most economists describe the U.S. economy as a mixed economy because private ownership operates alongside government regulation and public ownership of some industries.
Consumption is a social act: money and exchange are systems of symbolic exchange, so purchases carry shared cultural meaning rather than being purely private, economic choices.
Labor is the human input into the economy: people's effort, skill, and time are what owners hire and pay for to produce goods and services.

The U.S. economy distributes income unevenly: according to Pew Research Center analysis of Census data, the share of aggregate household income held by middle-income households fell from 62% in 1970 to 42% in 2020, while the share held by upper-income households rose from 29% to 50%.
Production is now globalized: global assembly lines assemble products over a series of international transactions, with design, components, assembly, and support spread across countries.
Employment has shifted toward services: per BLS employment projections, service-providing industries employed about 80% of U.S. workers in 2023 while goods-producing industries employed about 13%.

The economy is a social invention, not a law of nature: as a social institution it is human-made, varies across time and place, and can be reorganized, as seen in countries that have moved between state-run and market-based systems.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How to classify national economies: the capitalism/socialism pair vs. the market/command/mixed trio.
positions: OpenStax 3e presents capitalism and socialism as the dominant modern systems and notes that most economists call the United States a mixed economy.
Popular and textbook vocabulary also groups systems as market, command, and mixed.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names the three systems (market, command, mixed) descriptively, anchoring each definition in OpenStax 3e's attributed terms (private ownership with profit impetus; state ownership with equalizing aim; mixed), without endorsing any system.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Wording of the working definition of the economy differs across textbooks.
positions: OpenStax 3e: the social institution through which a society's resources (goods and services) are managed.
Common phrasing: the system through which societies produce, distribute, and consume goods and services.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the OpenStax 3e definition verbatim-attributed and explains that managing resources means producing, distributing, and consuming them, so both phrasings agree.
